articles.title: A 'multitasking mom' went viral at a baseball game. Her balancing act ignited a debate.
articles.summary: Many moms saw themselves in the woman's juggling act. Experts say: "Just because you can doesn't mean you should" do it all.
articles.body:
"The definition of a multitasking mother." "An Olympic champion." "Mom of the year."

These are the praises that ESPN commentators had not for an athlete — well, not a professional one, anyway — but for a woman in the stands at a San Francisco Giants game on Sept. 23. TV cameras found her expertly navigating the crowded stands while wearing a backpack and balancing three containers of food with her baby in a carrier strapped to her chest. She tiptoes to her seat next to a man who stands briefly as she sits down.

The camera cuts away for a moment, and the next shot shows the man eating his meal while the mom balances the remaining two trays of food on her lap and carefully unstraps her child from the carrier. "She'll be the last one to eat, too," one of the ESPN analysts says.

A 30-second clip of the multitasking mom went viral on TikTok , where commenters — largely women — saw themselves in her herculean solo efforts, took out some anger on the man next to her. "How do I divorce someone else's husband?" one asked, while another praised the ESPN analysts who "put him on BLAST."

Some took issue with how the sportscasters framed the situation, however well-intentioned they may have been. "A baseball game is being played, but the camera has found another endurance event in the stands," Olivia Howell wrote on Substack . The commentators are "calling the play-by-play while she performs it. Look at the balance. Look at the coordination. Look at the stamina. Look at mama go!"

But Howell says we are "watching a mother carry everybody's food back to a grown man while a sports commentator casually remarks that she will probably eat last." It's a line, she says, that has been "sitting in my stomach ever since."

Of course, a brief video of unwitting strangers lacks context and can easily be misconstrued. In her post, Howell imagined that the woman might respond by explaining that viewers had misunderstood the situation altogether. The mom in the video, Erika, recently reached out to Yahoo Creator Alesandra Dubin to share the real story behind the video: She had gone to the game with her husband to mark the loss of his close friend (who had played baseball). She wasn't hungry at the time, and her husband had offered to help every step of the way.

Still, the entire scene clearly struck a chord. The video is "like a Rorschach test," Barbara Greenberg , a psychologist specializing in parenting, family and teens, tells Yahoo. "We see an ink blot and then interpret what it is to us."

Erika may not have been what many online commenters called a " married single mom . " But what many women saw in the clip speaks to a familiar experience: the tendency for mothers to become the "default parent" in their relationships.

How did we get here? Why is the do-it-all mom such a familiar sight — and what would it take to lighten her load? We spoke to two psychologists to find out.

As the ESPN commentators noted, a woman who juggles work, motherhood and errands — in this case, a concession stand run with a baby in tow — can look like an ultra-capable "Olympic champion."

But, "sometimes competence becomes the punishment," Facebook user Rissa SoFar wrote in a response post. "The more capable you are, the more everybody around you starts treating your capability like unlimited capacity."

Greenberg says this reflects a common cultural stereotype: the "'super woman,'" she says. But appearing to have it all under control and actually feeling that way are not the same thing, she adds. Highly competent women, including Greenberg herself, may think: "I'll just take care of it myself because it'll get done well, and it will get done now," she admits. But, Thornton adds: "Just because you can doesn't mean you should ."

Until the middle of the 20th century, child-rearing and caring for the home were the typical full-time jobs of women. Structurally, we're long past that: Most women now work outside the home . More than half of moms and dads both worked full-time in 2025 , compared to just 31% in 1975. It's worth noting that men in the U.S. are doing more household labor than ever , at a record 100 minutes a day. But women are still doing 40 more minutes of chores per day than their male partners, and most parents agree that moms do the lion's share of child-care tasks .

But culturally, we haven't moved past the old norms. "The ways that mothers and fathers are socialized are very different," parenting psychologist Amber Thornton tells Yahoo. "If we're not careful and aware of the societal and cultural expectations that impact our families, we can accidentally fall into these roles that feel really prescribed and sometimes unequal."

The majority of child care and chores often fall on moms' plates. "In many cases, they've been the primary caregivers, so they continue with that role — and everything else" even while juggling work, says Greenberg. As a result, "a lot of women feel like they're carrying everything, literally and figuratively, like [the woman in the video] is," she adds.

Both psychologists I spoke to suggested that women might get more help from their partners if they ask for it. But, they also acknowledged that's part of the problem, because many women are already frustrated that "the onus is on them to change this dynamic," says Thornton.

That was the thesis of one scathing response video: "Women are married to men who are always happy to help," said Paige Connell , cohost of The Just Us Girls Podcast , in her Instagram post. "This is a guy who's probably happy to help….He would've gotten the food. All she had to do was ask," she says, sarcastically. Her point: Sure, many men will step up when asked. But why isn't taking on that work as intuitive to them as it is to women?

That's how many women become what Thornton describes as the default parent. "We shouldn't have to ask — we'd like to live a life where there's a natural consideration," she says. But, "a father may not realize and understand that; he may have to go through and [analyze] his own beliefs about what a mother is."

Thornton says that men need to ask themselves if their expectations for who does what at home are really fair. "Have those conversations with the women and mothers in your life," she advises men. "Talk to your partner, but also your mother about her experience and what she desired and some of the unspoken expectations she might have had."

Asking what you can do to help or, better yet, looking for an opportunity to pitch in and taking the initiative will "improve your partner's mental health," says Greenberg, "and it will make the family stronger, too."

Women, meanwhile, need to clearly communicate what their boundaries and needs are, Thornton says, "because if not, society has led us to believe that women have no limits and boundaries."

articles.title: Ex-India captain Asunta Lakra leads protest against Hockey India officials
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Former India women’s captain Asunta Lakra, along with a group of former national and international players, including Olympians, staged a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former India women’s captain Asunta Lakra, along with a group of former national and international players, including Olympians, staged a symbolic one-day protest against Hockey India secretary general Bholanath Singh and other office-bearers outside Gate No. 7 of the Major Dhyan Chand National Stadium here on Friday.The protesters, who had gathered at around 3pm, were also raising their voices against HI Director General Cdr R.K. Srivastava and treasurer Sekar J. Manoharan. The group demanded the formation of a sports ministry-backed ad-hoc committee to run the federation’s affairs until the next election.Asunta told TOI that the protest was initially planned at Jantar Mantar between 2pm and 4pm, but permission was denied by the police. The group subsequently assembled at the national stadium. Permission to protest at the main gate was also not granted, following which the protesters moved to Gate No. 7 and held their symbolic demonstration with placards before dispersing.The stadium complex houses offices of the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), including the Foreigners-I Division, Principal Accounts Office (Admn.) and Department of Border Management. Security at the premises is handled by the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF), which was cited in connection with the denial of permission for a protest inside the complex.Those attending the demonstration included Olympians Ashok Kumar, Romeo James, Vineet Kumar and Manohar Topno. Romeo James and Vineet Kumar were members of the Indian team at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics. Asian Games medallist Pramod Batlaw, along with former international players Bimal Lakra, Kanti Baa and Birendra Lakra, were also present.Asunta has previously accused Bholanath Singh of intimidation and harassment after she raised objections over the alleged harassment of young girls in Jharkhand. Following her allegations, the Indian Olympic Committee (IOA) constituted a probe panel to look into the matter.The protesting group sought an ad-hoc committee to oversee the federation until the next elections. articles.title: Asian Games: Anahat Singh, Abhay Singh lead India’s squash surge — two finals, three medals and Olympic spots in sight
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India enjoyed a remarkable day in squash at the Asian Games 2026 on Saturday, with Anahat Singh and Abhay Singh storming into the women’s and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India enjoyed a remarkable day in squash at the Asian Games 2026 on Saturday, with Anahat Singh and Abhay Singh storming into the women’s and men’s singles finals respectively, while the mixed doubles pairing of Joshna Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar secured a bronze medal at the Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena.The results gave India a shot at two squash gold medals on Sunday, while also putting Anahat and Abhay one victory away from potentially becoming India’s first squash players to secure direct qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.The Asian Games singles champions will earn direct LA28 qualification, subject to the eligibility criteria, including the PSA world ranking requirement at the qualification cut-off. Squash will make its Olympic debut in Los Angeles.It made Saturday one of the most productive days for Indian squash at a major continental event, with the country guaranteed three medals and still in contention for two golds.Asian Games Full Coverage | Medal Tally | ScheduleAnahat produces comeback for the agesThe biggest performance of the day came from 18-year-old Anahat, who pulled off one of the finest comebacks of her young career to defeat Japan's world No. 6 Satomi Watanabe 9-11, 11-13, 12-10, 11-6, 11-3.The world No. 17 Indian was staring at defeat after dropping the opening two games against the home favourite. Watanabe's variations, changes of pace and sharp angles had kept Anahat under constant pressure.But the teenager changed the complexion of the match in the third game.Trailing 8-10, Anahat saved two match points before producing a remarkable turnaround to win 12-10. She then carried the momentum into the fourth game, winning it 11-6 to level the contest.There was also an anxious moment during the semifinal when Anahat's head collided with Watanabe's shoulder while she attempted to retrieve the ball. The match was briefly stopped as the Indian received medical attention before returning to continue her fight.In the decider, Anahat gave Watanabe virtually no opportunity to regain control. She attacked with confidence and closed out the game 11-3 to complete a stunning 3-2 victory.The win was also revenge for Anahat, who had lost to Watanabe in another five-game contest earlier this year.Now she stands one victory away from an Asian Games gold medal — and potentially an Olympic ticket.Abhay follows Anahat into the gold-medal matchAbhay then completed India's singles double by powering past Pakistan's Muhammad Irfan 3-0 in the men's semifinal.The Indian won 11-3, 12-10, 11-6 in a 35-minute contest in which he controlled proceedings for long periods.Abhay made a fast start, racing to a 6-2 lead in the opening game before closing it out 11-3. Irfan pushed him harder in the second, but Abhay held his nerve in the tight moments to take it 12-10.There was no let-up in the third. Abhay maintained his control and closed out the match 11-6 to book his place in the final.Like Anahat, he is now one victory away from gold and a direct route to LA28. The Asian Games are the continental qualifying event for squash, with the men's and women's singles gold medallists earning Olympic qualification subject to the eligibility rules.Joshna and Velavan add a bronzeIndia's medal count in squash had already received a boost earlier in the day when Joshna Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar secured bronze in mixed doubles.The Indian pair lost a fiercely contested semifinal to Hong Kong's Tang Ming Hong and Lee Ka Yi 1-2 (10-11, 11-2, 10-11).After narrowly losing the opening game, Joshna and Velavan responded emphatically to level the contest by taking the second 11-2. The deciding game again went down to the wire, but the Hong Kong pair held their composure to win 11-10 and advance to the final.The bronze nevertheless marked another milestone for Joshna. Competing at a record seventh Asian Games, the 40-year-old added another medal to a collection that already included two silver and three bronze medals at the continental showpiece.India had assured itself of the mixed doubles medal after Joshna and Velavan defeated the Philippines' David Pelino and Jemyca Aribado in the quarterfinals on Friday.But Saturday's bigger story was the singles double.With Anahat and Abhay both through to the finals, India now has two chances to win squash gold and potentially secure two historic LA28 Olympic berths.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'You can't let the Olympic spot go by so quickly': Anahat Singh's stunning admission after 0-2 comeback
articles.summary: Indian teenager Anahat Singh produced a remarkable comeback against Japan’s higher-ranked Satomi Watanabe to reach the women’s singles final at the Asian
articles.body: Indian teenager Anahat Singh produced a remarkable comeback against Japan’s higher-ranked Satomi Watanabe to reach the women’s singles final at the Asian Games squash event on Saturday, while Abhay Singh also booked his place in the men’s singles title clash.Anahat and Abhay are now one win away from securing a spot at the 2028 Olympics, with the Asian Games men’s and women’s singles gold medallists earning direct qualification for the Games.The 18-year-old Anahat pulled off the biggest win of her career as she recovered from a two-game deficit to defeat world No. 6 Satomi 3-2 in a thrilling 51-minute semifinal at the Nagoya Kinjo-Futo Arena.Anahat won 9-11, 11-13, 12-10, 11-6, 11-3, exacting revenge for her previous five-game defeat against the Japanese player."The last time she won, I was 2-0 up and I ended up losing. And I mean, it was the other way around this time," Anahat said after the match.The prospect of an Olympic qualification spot was also on Anahat's mind as she fought her way back into the contest after falling two games behind."I do focus on that. It's something that I think of it more like something that's motivating rather than pressure. When I was losing, the first thought that came into my mind was you can't let the Olympic spot go by so quickly and you really need to push for it. That's what kept replaying in my head over and over and I think that's something that motivates me rather than pressure that you are supposed to be in the Olympics," Anahat said.Anahat had looked close to defeat after losing the opening two games. She had managed to draw level at 6-6 in the first before Satomi moved ahead and eventually closed it out 11-9.The second game followed a similar pattern. Anahat fought back from behind to level the score at 10-10 and then moved to 11-10, but Satomi responded strongly to win the next three points and take the game 13-11.The Indian then produced the turnaround that changed the match.Trailing 8-10 in the third game, Anahat won four straight points to take it 12-10. She carried that momentum into the fourth, where she again recovered from an early deficit to make it 6-6 before putting together five consecutive points to force a decider.Anahat's control, precision and well-executed drops continued to trouble Satomi, who struggled to regain the momentum she had established early in the match.The deciding game was largely one-way traffic. Anahat dominated the exchanges, produced at least three fine drops and capitalised on a series of unforced errors from Satomi to complete the comeback.The semifinal was briefly interrupted after the two players collided during the second game, with Anahat receiving medical attention."I bit my tongue. So it was bleeding, nothing serious," she said.Anahat, the junior world champion, will face Malaysia’s world No. 5 Sivasangari Subramaniam in Sunday’s final. Sivasangari defeated Hong Kong’s Chan Sin Yuk in the other semifinal."I still have a match left. If I end up playing the number one seed, she's a great player. I've played her numerous times before. I'm just excited to get on the court and see what I can do," said the junior world champion.Abhay sets up Malaysia clashAbhay Singh, meanwhile, had a relatively easier route to the final as he defeated Pakistan’s Muhammad Irfan 3-0 in 35 minutes.Abhay won 11-3, 12-10, 11-6 to make the title clash. He had earlier won gold in the men’s team event and bronze in mixed doubles at these Games."It was not an easy one. I think I did well to make it easy, but respect to your opponent. No Asian Games match is going to come easy," Abhay said later.He will take on Malaysia’s NG Eain Yow in Sunday’s final. NG Eain Yow defeated Pakistan’s Zaman Noor in the other semifinal."I think all the people listening to you love the India-Pakistan stuff, but for us it's just another opponent, just another match. Too many people put too much work into us, you have to come in and do them justice."Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Assefa vuelve al maratón de Berlín para asaltar un récord mundial bajo 'sospecha'
articles.standfirst: La etíope regresa al escenario de su plusmarca universal de 2023 para intentar batir el posterior registro de 2.09:56 que estableció Chepngetich, ahora suspendida por dopaje
articles.summary: La etíope regresa al escenario de su plusmarca universal en 2023 para acercarse al registro de 2.09:56 que estableció Chepngetich, ahora suspendida por dopaje
articles.body: Tigst Assefa regresa este domingo a las calles de Berlín, donde hace tres años estableció el récord del mundo femenino de maratón, con una marca de 2.11:53. Ahora la etíope es la tercera atleta en el ranking de todos los tiempos, ya que fue superada por su compatriota Tesfay (2.10:51 en Barcelona este año) y la keniata Ruth Chepngetich, ahora suspendida por dopaje, que corrió en 2.09:56 en Chicago en 2024. La subcampeona olímpica y mundial es uno de los grandes focos de esta edición de la carrera alemana, que en categoría masculina había anunciado a Sebastian Sawe, plusmarquista mundial y primer atleta en bajar de las 2.00:00 en maratón, que finalmente es baja por lesión. Tampoco estará al final Kenenisa Bekele, que tenía previsto volver a la capital germana a sus 44 años, pero también se ha lesionado en uno de los últimos entrenamientos. Assefa se erige, por tanto, en la gran favorita y busca su tercer triunfo consecutivo en Berlín. Compite por primera vez desde su victoria en el último maratón de Londres, en el que estableció un récord mundial sólo en carrera de mujeres con un tiempo de 2.15:41 en abril. “Tengo muchas ganas de volver a correr en el rápido circuito de Berlín y espero poder continuar con mi racha de éxitos este domingo”, aseguró. “Estoy muy bien preparada y quiero lograr mi mejor marca personal”. Entre sus rivales, habrá siete mujeres con marcas inferiores 2.20:00. Entre ellas se encuentran la keniana Rosemary Wanjiru, que defiende su título del pasado año, y la etíope Dera Dida, compañera de entrenamiento de Assefa y subcampeona en Berlín el año pasado. Sin Sawe en liza, la carrera masculina se presenta más abierta que nunca. El tanzano Gabriel Geay, con una marca personal de 2.03:00, es el que encabeza la lista de favoritos en Berlín, junto a los etíopes Guye Adola, Shura Kitata y Getaneh Molla. De hecho, Adola buscará recuperar el título que ya ganó en 2021. El atleta de 35 años estableció su mejor marca personal de 2.03:46 en Berlín en 2017, pero estuvo cerca de igualarla al ganar en Rotterdam en abril con un tiempo de 2.03:54. En la lista de participantes también figuran Selemon Barega, campeón olímpico de 10.000 metros en 2021, que terminó séptimo en el maratón de Tokio en marzo (2.05:00), así como el keniano Erick Sang, que corrió en 2.05:34 en la carrera de Rotterdam, ganada por Adola.

articles.title: Lindsey Vonn, French Skiier Matthieu Bailet Reveal Relationship with New Photos from Summer Vacation
articles.summary: Three-time Olympic medalist Lindsey Vonn confirmed her relationship with French skier Matthieu Bailet on social media.
articles.body:
Three-time Olympic medalist Lindsey Vonn confirmed her relationship with French skier Matthieu Bailet on social media.

Vonn posted a series of photos on Instagram this week summing up her summer. She included multiple shots of herself and Bailet together.

The 41-year-old certainly earned the right to have a relaxing break given the ordeal she experienced this past winter. She ruptured her ACL prior to the 2026 Winter Olympics and then suffered a complex leg fracture while competing in the Milan Cortina Games.

Vonn said in August she was still in the recovery phase with another surgery ahead.

articles.title: Olympics: Germany picks Munich for Summer Games bid
articles.summary: Since the last time the Summer Games were on German soil in 1972, Germany has launched seven unsuccessful bids to host.
articles.body:
Munich has been selected ahead of the Cologne/Rhine-Ruhr region by the German Olympic Committee (DOSB) as part of a bid to host the 2036, 2040 or 2044 Olympic Games.

The decision was announced by German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Saturday in the southwestern spa town of Baden-Baden.

Launched as a race between four candidates, the DOSB was given a choice between two after Berlin withdrew on Thursday and Hamburg’s withdrawal in May.

“We’re thinking about all of Germany,” Bavarian state premier Markus Soeder said on stage after Munich’s successful bid was announced.

“The Cologne bid made things really tough for us and pretty tense until the end.

“I want that we work jointly to bring the games to Germany. It is a chance at something historic, and we want to give everything to present ourselves as a united country – from north to south and from east to west.

“That’s our goal and what we’re working towards. Thank you for the trust.”

The Munich bid centres on the Olympic Park in the north of the city. Built for the 1972 Games, it has undergone extensive renovations in recent years.

In a statement issued moments after the announcement, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz congratulated Munich.

“Germany has an Olympic candidate. Munich will enter the race on our behalf, and I warmly congratulate the state capital and the Free State of Bavaria on this,” he said.

“Now, together with our Olympic candidate, we eagerly look forward to this major event … Germany is ready for the Olympics.”

In order to shore up support for the bid, Munich held a referendum in late 2025. Almost two-thirds (66.4 percent) of voters cast their ballot in support of hosting the Games, on a turnout of 44 percent.

The positive result was a stark contrast to previous Olympic referenda, with votes to host the 2022 Winter Games in Munich or the 2024 Summer Games in Hamburg failing to win support.

Hamburg’s hopes to be chosen as a potential host city by the DOSB for the 2036, 2040 or 2044 Games were undermined by a negative public consultation, while another hopeful, Berlin, decided against holding a referendum.

The DOSB is set to begin a “continuous dialogue” process with the IOC in the run-up to a shortlisting process in March 2027.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) will designate one or more preferred hosts in late 2028, with an eventual bid to be selected by the IOC in mid 2029.

Since the last time the Summer Games were on German soil in 1972, Germany has launched seven unsuccessful bids to again play host.

If the bid is successfully chosen by the IOC, it will be the third time Germany has hosted the Olympics. Berlin hosted the Games in 1936 with Germany then under Nazi leadership, while Munich played host to the 1972 Games, then as part of West Germany.

The 1972 edition in Munich was marred by the attack on the Israeli delegation in the Olympic Village, which resulted in the deaths of 11 members of the Israeli Olympic team.

The only other Games held on German soil were the 1936 Winter Games, held in the southern town of Garmisch-Partenkirchen.

articles.title: Dramático final para Assefa en Berlín: entra en meta cojeando tras rozar el récord mundial de maratón
articles.standfirst: La etíope, que fue a ritmo de plusmarca universal más de 35 kilómetros, se lesiona al final y se impone en 2.11:04, tercer mejor registro de siempre en la distancia
articles.summary: La etíope, que fue a ritmo de plusmarca universal más de 35 kilómetros, se lesiona al final y se impone en 2.11:04, tercer mejor registro de siempre en la distancia
articles.body: Tigst Assefa escribió en Berlín una historia con tintes de hazaña, sufrimiento y dramatismo. La etíope, que ya en 2023 batió en estas calles el récord del mundo de la distancia, coqueteó durante más de 35 kilómetros con una estratosférica plusmarca mundial con la que quería borrar de lo más alto del ranking de siempre el 'dudoso' registro de la keniata Ruth Chepngetich, ahora suspendida por dopaje, que corrió en 2.09:56 en Chicago en 2024. Hizo lo más difícil: correr a ritmo de récord del mundo durante la mayor parte del maratón con una soltura de dejaba claro el potencial y la calidad que atesora la subcampeona olímpica y mundial. Pero el maratón, la distancia que ha dejado algunos de los capítulos más duros de la historia del atletismo, no perdona ni a los mejores. Y Assefa vivió en sus piernas esa dureza cuando a falta de pocos kilómetros para meta empezó a sufrir y cojear, con calambres que le impidieron poder mantener ese récord que había saboreado hasta el final. Porque Berlín, acostumbrada a poner 'nombre' a muchos de los mejores registros mundiales de la distancia (13 se habían batido en su historia hasta este domingo), quería recuperar esa posición de privilegio -que ahora estaba depositada en Londres y Chicago- en alguna de sus categorías y, ante la baja de Sawe, la apuesta era la carrera femenina, con Tigst Assefa. La etíope, que había realizado su mejor maratón por las calles berlinesas en 2023 con 2.11:53, salió a por todas para asaltar esa difícil empresa que firmó Chepngetich (2.09:56 en Chicago en 2024). Así, y pese a que no pudo coger el primer avituallamiento, la etíope, bien secundada por las liebres contratadas para la ocasión, alcanzó el kilómetro 10 en 30:48, por debajo del récord mundial. La keniata Rosemary Wanjiru, segunda, ya avanzaba a más de un minuto de la líder (31:53). Assefa protagonizó entonces una carrera contra ella misma, el crono... y la historia. Pasó el kilómetro 15 en 46:13 y el medio maratón en 1.04:57, con una proyección en ese momento de 2.09:53 al final, siempre por debajo del tiempo universal. Llegaba la gran prueba de fuego, el segundo medio maratón que definiría si esa cadencia de Assefa sería suficiente para citarse con la historia. Por detrás, su primera perseguidora corría ya a más de 3 minutos al paso del kilómetro 25, que la etíope había pasado en 1.17:00, mientras que su compatriota Dida lo hacía en 1.20:22. Poco después, Tigst volvió a tener problemas en otro de los avituallamientos, donde no pudo coger la botella, pero no parecía sufrir las consecuencias de ello: seguía volando hacia el récord. Pasó el kilómetro 30 a 1:32:15, aún rodeada del grupo de cinco liebres, y el 35, a 1.47:32: apenas siete kilómetros separaban a Assefa de la historia. Con una liebre menos en el grupo, en el que se incrementaban las consultas a los relojes para comprobar si la hazaña aún era posible, la subcampeona olímpica y mundial mantuvo su cadencia de récord. Pero aún quedaba sufrimiento. Los últimos kilómetros se hicieron interminables para Assefa, que empezó a sufrir las consecuencias del estratosférico ritmo... y quizás de la falta de líquidos. Su rictus denotaba ese padecimiento, con zancadas más pesadas, cojeando. Las liebres tenían que esperarla, y ni siquiera el tiempo que había logrado atesorar de ventaja fue salvavidas suficiente para mantener ese récord mundial. Renqueante, con calambres, sin apenas poder correr, cruzó la meta en 2.11:04, marca personal y tercer mejor registro de siempre en la distancia. Un botín insuficiente para una carrera que había sido antológica hasta casi el final. La etíope Hirpa llegó segunda, con 2.16:53, a cinco minutos de la ganadora, mientras que completó el podio la también etíope Dida, con 2.16:55. Sin el plusmarquista mundial, Sabastian Sawe, en liza por lesión, las miradas de la carrera masculina recaían en el grupo formado por el tanzano Gabriel Geay, que con una marca personal de 2.03:00 llegaba como el más rápido de los participantes, junto a los etíopes Guye Adola, Shura Kitata y Getaneh Molla. Y fueron ellos, también con el keniata Sang o el etíope Belihu, los que dominaron en cabeza los primeros kilómetros. El grupo de favoritos siguió compacto durante muchos kilómetros. Alcanzó el medio maratón en 1.01:01, con el keniata Sang en cabeza, por delante de la 'Armada' etíope, con Barega, Belihu y Kitata, entre ellos. El kilómetro 30 marcó el primer cambio importante en la carrera masculina. Los etíopes Adola, Barega, y Diriba incrementaron el ritmo, un movimiento que sus rivales no pudieron responder. Pero aún Adola, acompañado por Kiptoo en labores de liebre, tenía un cambio más y se situó solo en cabeza para jugarse la victoria en los kilómetros finales. A partir de ahí fue un paseo para Adola, que sólo tuvo que garantizar su ritmo para alcanzar la meta en 2.02:51. Segundo fue el etíope Diriba, con 2.03:19, mientras que completó el podio el tanzano Geay, con 2.03:59.

articles.title: Berlin Marathon 2026: Tigst Assefa barely misses women's world record after sustaining injury late in race
articles.summary: The Ethiopian runner still won in a course-record time.
articles.body:
Ethiopia's Tigst Assefa finished just short of the world record in the women's marathon after she began to limp in the final mile of the Berlin Marathon on Sunday, still winning in a course-record time of 2 hours, 11 minutes and 4 seconds.

The time was a personal best for Assefa but just off the WR time of 2:09:56 set by Kenya's Ruth Chepngetich at the 2024 Chicago Marathon. Assefa, 29, was under that pace for much of Sunday's race until she began limping. After passing the 35-kilometer mark in 1:47:32, Assefa was on pace to finish in 2:09:38, 18 seconds faster than Chepngetich's record time.

Assefa still finished with the third-fastest time ever in the women's marathon, trailing only Chepngetich and Ethiopian Fotyen Tesfay's 2:10:51. Assefa ran a 2:11:53 in 2023 in Berlin — then a world record and now the fourth-fastest time ever — and said she was "excited to once again try to break the world record" prior to this year's race.

Just five months earlier, Assefa broke her own record for a women's-only marathon by winning the London Marathon in a time of 2:15:41.

Chepngetich is serving a three-year suspension for doping violations after she tested positive for a banned diuretic in March 2025.

Assefa made it an Ethiopian sweep in Berlin after Guye Adola won the men's race in 2:02:51. He previously won Berlin in 2021. Ethiopia's Gemechu Dirib was second with Tanzania's Gabriel Geay in third.

Kenya's Sabastian Sawe, who became the first person to run a sub-two-hour marathon when he broke the men's WR in London earlier this year, did not run in Berlin on Sunday because of an injury.

Berlin is a flat course that runners target for fast times. Overcast skies also made for ripe conditions for an attempt at the world record after race organizers moved up the start time to avoid the hot temperatures at last year's marathon.

articles.title: Franklin wins three canoe medals at European championships
articles.summary: Olympic medallist Mallory Franklin completes her return following the birth of her daughter with canoe gold and kayak cross silver at the Paddle Europe Slalom Championships in Ivrea.
articles.body:
Olympic medallist Mallory Franklin completed her return to action by winning canoe gold and kayak cross silver at the Paddle Europe Slalom Championships in Ivrea.

The 32-year-old delivered a flawless, penalty-free run of 100.47 seconds to beat France's Doriane Delassus by 0.03 seconds and claim her third career European C1 title.

Victory marked Franklin's first individual medal since the birth of her daughter, having opened her week in Italy with a bronze medal in the team event.

"It's a really nice way to end the year. It's been a tough one coming back and getting back on the start line," said Franklin.

"I've been building throughout the year and it's just a nice way to finish it."

Franklin went on to complete a full set of medals on the final day, battling through the kayak cross knockout rounds under the floodlights to secure silver behind the Czech Republic's Tereza Kneblova.

Great Britain enjoyed double success in the kayak cross as two-time Olympic medallist Kimberley Woods took individual gold, winning the morning time trial in 48.02 seconds ahead of Poland's Klaudia Zwolinska.

And there was bronze in the men's K1 team event for Ben Haylett, Sam Leaver and Joe Clarke, to go with the one won by Woods, Franklin and Ellis Miller in the women's C1.

In the men's events, Clarke and Sam Leaver missed out on the podium in the kayak final, finishing fifth and sixth respectively behind Czech winner Jakub Krejci.

articles.title: Berlin Marathon: Tigst Assefa wins but injury halts world record time
articles.summary: Ethiopian runner Tigst Assefa wins the Berlin Marathon but narrowly misses out on breaking the women's world record because of injury.
articles.body:
An injured Tigst Assefa hobbled over the line at the Berlin Marathon on Sunday after looking set to smash the women's world record.

The Ethiopian still won with the third-fastest time in history in two hours 11 minutes four seconds.

But the 29-year-old, a silver medallist at the Paris Olympics two years ago, had been cruising to a new record before fading in the final stages.

Kenyan athlete Ruth Chepngetich's time of 2:09:56, set at the 2024 Chicago Marathon, remains the world record time, though that result is overshadowed by the three-year doping ban she received in 2025.

Assefa, the 2026 London Marathon winner, started rapidly and led the field by a minute at the 15km mark. She was ahead of the record pace at 35km and is a renowned fast finisher - but began to suffer clear discomfort and her pace slowed.

However she still broke the Berlin course record of 2:11:53 that she set in 2023 - which was also her previous personal best.

In addition, she improved on her time of 2:15:41 at the London Marathon earlier this year.

"We have to bow our heads to this performance. She was on a world record course for most of the race but then something happened to her tendon," said race director Mark Milde.

"To finish like this, I've never seen something like this. The pain is hard to imagine.

"With a heavy heart, we saw her set a course record, but it could have been a lot more."

The top five finishers were all from Ethiopia, with Bedatu Hirpa second and Dera Dida third.

Guye Adola - another Ethiopian - won the men's race with a time of 2:02:50.

articles.title: Cumple su sueño de correr el maratón de Berlín con 84 años... ¡y acaba en 4.40:58!
articles.standfirst: El sudafricano Johannes Maros Mosehla, que se convirtió en 2023 en el atleta de más edad en acabar el Comrades Marathon, quería correr un maratón en el extranjero
articles.summary: El sudafricano Johannes Maros Mosehla quería correr un maratón en el extranjero
articles.body: Son muchas las historias que se entremezclan en los 42,195 kilómetros de cada maratón... y el de Berlín, uno de los 'majors' más populares entre los 'runners', en uno de los que atesora hazañas, retos, promesas, drama... Más allá del dramático final que protagonizó Tigst Assefa, que entró cojeando tras lesionarse en los últimos kilómetros después de haber corrido a ritmo de récord del mundo toda la carrera, destacó la proeza de un atleta, Johannes Maros Mosehla, que cumplió su sueño de correr un maratón fuera de Sudáfrica... ¡con 84 años! Mosehla, que en 2023 se convirtió en el corredor de más edad en acabar el Comrades Marathon -una prueba ultra de 90 kilómetros-, quería disputar un maratón lejos de su tierra natal y apostó por hacerlo en Berlín. “Durante años he dicho que mi nombre es conocido en todo el mundo gracias a mis hazañas como corredor y me encantaría ir a correr al extranjero para que puedan ver quién es este viejo”, decía Mosehla a un medio local antes de viajar hacia Alemania. Y Johannes cumplió su sueño con creces. Acabó el maratón de Berlín en 4.40:58, una medalla muy especial para el corredor octogenario, que se había mostrado orgulloso de que su participación pudiera inspirar a otras personas a perseguir sus metas sin importar la edad.

articles.standfirst: La etíope, que fue a ritmo de récord del mundo hasta los kilómetros finales, hizo los últimos metros cojeando y las pruebas revelan ahora que sufre la rotura parcial del tendón de Aquiles
articles.summary: La etíope, que fue a ritmo de récord del mundo hasta los kilómetros finales, hizo los últimos metros cojeando y las pruebas revelan ahora que sufre la rotura parcial del tendón de Aquiles
articles.body: Tras correr 40 kilómetros de una forma memorable, a ritmo de un récord del mundo que hubiera enterrado la dudosa marca lograda por Ruth Chepngetich en 2024 (2.09:56), Tigst Assefa vivió el drama de la distancia en primera persona, al sufrir problemas físicos que le impidieron mantener al final la cadencia con la que había volado hacia la historia. Y así, cojeando, con ostensibles gestos de dolor, logró cruzar la meta en 2.11:04, tercera mejor marca de siempre, para desplomarse posteriormente con el rictus desencajado. Rápidamente recibió la ayuda de varias personas, entre ellos el legendario Haile Gebrselassie, que sostuvieron a la etíope, con problemas para andar. Ahora, según informó el director de la carrera, Mark Milde, a AFP, las primeras pruebas revelan que la etíope acabó el maratón con una rotura parcial del tendón de Aquiles de su pierna derecha, una importante lesión que podría alejar a la atleta de la competición durante un tiempo.

articles.title: Game #162: Astros at Athletics Game Thread
articles.summary: One more time
articles.body:
We made it folks! The final game of the season is upon us. The A's are set to suit up one final time this season, taking on the Astros to wrap up the year. The A's stand at 64-97, sitting in fourth place in the AL West and with the second-worst record in the American League. That's where they'll sit this offseason but if the team can end the year with a win that'd send us into the offseason on a high note. Let's finish the year with a 65th win in front of Sacramento.

As for Houston , this isn't just any game for them. They still have not clinched a spot in the postseason as they enter today tied with the Texas Rangers at 80-81 atop the AL West. Thanks to them owning the tie breaker the Astros control their own fate: win and they're win. The Rangers will be watching this game and rooting for our A's, hoping to keep their playoff hopes alive. They need to pair their own win with an Astros loss to make it to October. In a way it's up to the A's which Texas team goes to the postseason. Which would you prefer to allow to stay alive a bit longer? Either is a bad pick.

Taking the ball today in the final to start things off is right-handed reliever Seth Johnson. That means we're looking at a bullpen game today. Johnson as you may remember was the lone acquisition at the mid-season trade deadline, coming over from Philadelphia in exchange for outfielder Colby Thomas . Johnson has split time between the big league club and the Aviators in the two months since joining the organization, posting a 6.89 ERA in 11 appearances at the big league level. We shouldn't expect more than an inning or two out of the righty this afternoon, and from there it'll be all Kotsay mixing and matching.

Here's the final A's lineup of the 2026 season:

Not how we thought the last lineup of the season would look but six months of baseball will grind down plenty of teams. It's been the typical lineup here down the stretch and they've been servicable, especially since the return of Langeliers. We'll also get to see infielder Joshua Kuroda-Grauer one more time this afternoon, and it's a great sign and he'll be able to put that nasty injury he suffered fully behind him heading into winter. And another good sign, catcher Brian Serven is back in there after taking a ball of the face earlier in the week.

The Astros meanwhile, with their season on the line, have right-hander Peter Lambert taking the ball this afternoon. Lambert has been a godsend for the Astros this season. An offseason pickup from Colorado , the 29-year-old has broken out with a 3.87 ERA in a team-leading 28 starts, solidifying a shaky Astros rotation. Houston isn't in contention or anywhere near the top of the division without his emergence, and he's a likely option for Game Two if the Astros advance to the playoffs.

Time to finish the season. Wrap it up with a win, boys. Let's go A's!

articles.title: Charlotte Henrich: Olympic dream a 'real possibility' for rising star
articles.summary: Welsh 400m athlete Charlotte Henrich has her sights set on Los Angeles having found her confidence with a breakthrough summer in 2026.
articles.body:
Just 12 months ago, 400-metre runner Charlotte Henrich was celebrating European Under-20 gold in Finland.

Fast forward a year and Henrich is no longer a promising young talent knocking on the door of senior athletics, but an athlete making her mark on the biggest tracks.

Ever since winning bronze with Great Britain in her first senior appearance at the World Athletics Relays in May, she has added accolades in her debut season.

The 20-year-old has become a Welsh record holder, a European Championship and Ultimate Championship silver medallist, and a Commonwealth Games finalist.

And now, Henrich has her sights firmly set on the biggest stage of all - the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles.

"I really want to go," Henrich told BBC Sport. "Even at Paris 2024, I never watched that event thinking that I could be there.

"I don't think I ever let myself dream that I could be there, and now it feels like a real possibility."

Born in France and raised in Kent after moving to England aged five, Henrich qualifies to represent Wales through her family, who hail from Carmarthen.

Her heritage allowed her to compete for Wales at the Commonwealth Games, where she finished fourth this summer, narrowly missing out on a medal.

Family support has been central to her success so far. By her own admission, she has grappled with self-doubt throughout her young career.

"In school I was very behind and I felt like everyone was a lot better than me," she admitted.

"Every single day I used to come home and say to my dad, 'I am rubbish at everything'.

"Now it's really nice to tell myself that I'm definitely not rubbish at everything."

After winning 400m gold at the 2022 European Under-18 Championships, Henrich felt she placed a "lot of unnecessary pressure" on herself.

"When you do well in your junior career, it can have a bit of a negative effect on your performance because you are so desperate to keep proving," she said.

"After under-18s, everyone was like 'you're under-18 European Champ!', and I didn't want to hear it. I didn't feel that I deserved it."

And though Henrich can now look back on those victories with pride, there are still moments when the youngster feels uneasy.

"It feels a bit abnormal and a bit weird," she said. "It's like, is that me? It feels like the things I've achieved, it's not me who has done it.

"It's just like this person's done this and I'm just here.

"I was talking to Amy [Hunt] at the end of Europeans in the lobby, and I was like, 'you're so cool, you've got four gold medals [at the Commonwealth Games]'."

"She told me that I am on this team as well. It was nice that I wasn't just a spectator."

How the race they said women couldn't run took centre stage

Sweeney ad a barrier for girls in sport - Hunt

You would be forgiven for thinking that Henrich's debut season on the senior stage has extinguished any remaining doubt about her ability on the track.

And with so many achievements packed into one season, it is no surprise that she is still trying to process it herself.

It was her impressive anchor leg that earned Great Britain silver in the mixed 4x400 relay at September's Ultimate Championship in Budapest.

That eye-catching result closed out a season in which Henrich shaved over a second off her 400m personal best and proved to herself that she belongs among the best.

"I'm quite proud of the way I manoeuvred it," she said of her silver medal-winning leg in Hungary.

"I was running and I was thinking that I could overtake her. I just had to stay strong.

"When you're on the track, you just kind of go into autopilot. That bit isn't stressful."

Henrich's nod of self-confidence began at the British Championships in June, where she set a Welsh 400m record for the first time.

Having started the year targeting a sub-51 second 400m sprint, Henrich clocked 50.58 to finish third in Birmingham.

In doing so, she beat Michelle Scutt's 44-year record, only to break it again less than a month later by running 0.13 seconds faster at the Diamond League event in London.

"It's been quite an unexpected year," Henrich admitted. "I've definitely gone above and beyond what I thought I could do.

"I knew that this year was going to be hard because the jump was always going to be big."

She said she really believed in herself after the British Championships.

"I ran a big PB, and I was like, 'this is great'," she added.

"I know that I'm still young and there are things that I'll hopefully improve. I'm working really well with my coach.

"This year has been very much me saying, 'let's see what we can do,' and now I've got the experience."

Now Henrich hopes for a "really exciting" future, with her focus firmly on the Los Angeles Olympics, where Wales' rising sprinting star is even allowing herself the chance to dream.

"A lot of people are too scared to dream because if it doesn't happen, it's going to be a big disappointment," she said.

"But now it's cool that I can say I want to be in LA. If I'm not in LA, then I'm going to be so disappointed.

"I've been thinking about LA a lot, and I think I will be thinking about LA for the next two years.

"It would mean a lot, especially because I've been dreaming about this since I was a kid."

articles.title: How waste food helps West Midlands families through the week
articles.summary: The scheme runs in schools across the West Midlands, including Birmingham and Walsall.
articles.body:
Food that would otherwise be thrown away by supermarkets is helping to feed hundreds of families and schoolchildren through a community meal scheme.

Charity FoodCycle said its programme turns surplus supermarket produce into free meals and groceries for families, helping to cut waste while easing household costs.

Among the schools taking part is Ark Tindal Academy in Balsall Heath, Birmingham, where families go to a weekly community meal and children take part in activities before dinner is served.

Families are given a free vegetarian meal as well as groceries to take home.

"It's a free meal in the week, and then they get a bag of groceries to take home with them, which some parents have said has been really helpful," said FoodCycle's Sophie Aoun.

She said the meals were also designed to introduce children to a wider range of fruit and vegetables.

Teacher Amy Henderson, from the academy, said the scheme had helped ease pressure on families facing rising household bills.

"With the cost of living, we know how expensive things are today, and it really does take pressure off the families," she said.

"It's really heart-warming to know that they have had a good meal."

Henderson said the sessions also helped parents, children, school staff and volunteers build relationships.

"It's a really lovely social event," she added.

FoodCycle collects surplus produce from supermarkets and uses it to prepare meals and provide groceries for families.

The initiative runs at schools across the West Midlands including Windsor Olympic Academy in Birmingham and Goldsmiths Primary Academy in Walsall.

"Our hope is that by turning surplus food into these free community meals we're doing more than just filling plates for an evening," Aoun said.

articles.title: Asian Games: Manu Bhaker returns empty-handed after four medal events as India’s shooting campaign falls short of Hangzhou
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Double Olympic medallist Manu Bhaker will return from the Asian Games 2026 without a medal after competing in four events in Aichi-Nagoya,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Double Olympic medallist Manu Bhaker will return from the Asian Games 2026 without a medal after competing in four events in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan — an unexpected outcome for one of India’s biggest medal hopes and another indication of the shooting contingent’s struggles to match its record haul from the previous edition.India had won 22 shooting medals, including seven gold, at the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023. In Aichi-Nagoya, the Indian shooters have so far managed 12 medals, with only one gold, with just five trap medal events remaining in the competition. Esha Singh’s silver in the women’s 25m pistol on Monday added to the tally, but the overall campaign has lacked the gold-medal returns India had hoped for.Manu’s four-event campaign ends without a podiumManu entered the Games as one of India’s biggest medal contenders after her historic double bronze at the Paris Olympics and strong recent international form. But the 24-year-old could not convert her four medal opportunities into a podium finish.Her campaign began with the women’s 10m air pistol events. Manu qualified third for the individual final with 579 points but finished fifth after scoring 181.1 in the medal round. India also narrowly missed a medal in the corresponding team event, finishing fourth.Asian Games Full Coverage | Medal Tally | ScheduleThe 25m pistol events offered another opportunity, but Manu missed the individual final after scoring 579-18x in qualification to finish 11th. She then ended her campaign on Monday as India finished fifth in the 25m pistol team event.The Indian trio of Esha Singh, Manu and Rahi Sarnobat scored 1727-56x. China won gold with 1743-68x, South Korea took silver with 1735-65x and Chinese Taipei claimed bronze with 1734-48x.Esha provided a bright spot by winning silver in the individual 25m pistol final after an exhausting series of shoot-offs, giving India another shooting medal.ALSO READ: 0 points! How a rare, inexplicable miss cost India a 25m pistol team medalShooting still one of India’s biggest medal contributor, but gold returns lagDespite Manu’s disappointment, shooting remains one of India’s most productive disciplines at Aichi-Nagoya. The contingent has delivered 12 medals so far, but the haul includes only one gold, a sharp contrast to the seven gold medals and 22 total shooting medals India collected at Hangzhou.Manu had arrived in Japan in good form. She won bronze at the 2026 ISSF World Cup in Hangzhou, while Esha claimed gold in the women’s 25m pistol at the same event. At the ISSF World Cup in Munich, Manu also won silver in the 10m air pistol mixed team event with Samrat Rana. She subsequently won individual silver in the women’s 25m pistol at the Asian Shooting Championships.Her father, Ram Kishan Bhaker, acknowledged that her performance had fallen below the standards she had established.“Manu's performance was not as per her standard because she set a very high standard and expectation for the Indian fans. As per my expectations, her score must be more than 585; it should be more than 585 to 595. Today's score was not enough...” he told IANS.He also questioned the circumstances surrounding Rahi Sarnobat’s crucial miss in the 25m pistol qualification.“Rahi was shooting very well, but suddenly one shot was not showing, which I believe may be the technical glitch or something else.”“But, later on the jury said that the shot went out of target, which certainly I don't believe, because Rahi is a very experienced shooter, and it could be something else. Let the jury test what it is or otherwise everything was going well,” he added.With five trap medal events still to come, India can add to its shooting tally. articles.title: María de Valdés, la historia de una ausencia, un homenaje y un podio de lágrimas
articles.standfirst: La nadadora, que perdió a su padre en 2023, fue segunda en la Copa de España de aguas abiertas de los Juegos del Agua que se disputan en Melilla
articles.summary: La nadadora, que perdió a su padre en 2023, fue segunda en la Copa de España de aguas abiertas de los Juegos del Agua que se disputan en Melilla
articles.body: Esta es una historia de resiliencia. Corría el año 2023 y para nuestra protagonista no era un momento cualquiera. Necesitaba afrontar el año olímpico a tope para sacarse la espinita de no haber podido debutar en los Juegos de Tokio. Pero un golpe del destino le arrebató a su padre. Su vida quedó en penumbra y sus ilusiones deportivas, aparcadas. Había un Mundial en febrero de 2024, en Doha, era la puerta olímpica. Aprobó el examen, claro, y ahora, dos años después, ha logrado un segundo puesto en la Copa de España de aguas abiertas de los Juegos del Agua, que comenzaron este domingo en Melilla. María de Valdés (Fuengirola, 1998) llegó emocionalmente tocada al Campeonato del Mundo de Aguas Abiertas en Doha. Su irreparable pérdida tres meses antes era un arma de doble filo para unos 10 kilómetros con las grandes estrellas mundiales jugándose diez plazas. Pero María quería intentarlo, por ella, pero sobre todo por su padre… La malagueña se plantó en la salida de una carrera frente a las mejores nadadoras del mundo y no solo no se arrugó, sino que más que nadar, ‘levitaba’ por las aguas de Doha. Aguas donde las corrientes y las mareas no lo ponían fácil. María estaba obsesionada por estar desde el principio en el grupo cabecero porque las diez plazas tenían el billete para los Juegos de París. La dura preparación invernal en altura y el desgarro familiar actuaban como dos martillos en su cabeza. Estaba preparada físicamente –“tenía que aguantar de principio a fin, lo tenía en la cabeza. Se jugaban trece plazas, quería estar siempre entre las diez primeras porque sabía que si me descolgaba no iba a poder recuperar. Esa ha sido la estrategia”, argumentaba. Los últimos kilómetros fueron de resistencia, de resiliencia pura. En cada brazada el recuerdo de su padre fue un acicate y espoleó aún más a la malagueña, que se iba a jugar nada menos que el oro con Sharon. Les separó la foto-finish pero, más allá del oro o la plata, María había hecho historia y le había hecho el mejor homenaje posible a su progenitor: “Estoy aún que no me lo creo, super emocionada y lo primero se lo quiero dedicar a mi padre que ha fallecido hace tres meses, a toda mi familia que me está apoyando desde España, a mi entrenador Jesús (de la Fuente, técnico del CN Liceo de La Coruña) y a todo el staff de España que me están apoyando”. Tras su gesta, las lágrimas inundaron su cara en un primer abrazo en el pantalán con su compañera Ángela Martínez, cuando salió desfondada de una carrera para la historia. Aquella medalla cuyas lágrimas inundaron el podio no solo le dio el billete olímpico para París 2024, también le dio un enorme impulso para el siguiente ciclo. Hoy, María es una nadadora experimentada y consolidada en el top 5 del ranking mundial y es una de las grandes estrellas de los Juegos del Agua Melilla 2026.

articles.title: Olympic and Wembley Park executives appointed to Marlow Studios
articles.summary: Sir John Armitt is appointed chairman and Wembley Park leader Max James becomes chief executive.
articles.body:
Two executives who helped deliver the 2012 Olympics and create Wembley Park have been appointed to lead Marlow Studios.

The Buckinghamshire film studio is expected to support more than 2,000 jobs during its 44-month construction, with preliminary work having begun earlier this year.

Sir John Armitt, who chaired the Olympic Delivery Authority, has been appointed chairman, while Max James has become chief executive.

James led the creation and delivery of major mixed-use developments in London, including Wembley Park, Greenwich Peninsula and Thameside West.

Former chief executive and co-founder Robert Laycock will step down and become a non-executive member of the board.

Armitt said: "The Studios' construction is a strong vote of confidence in the UK creative and technology sectors, reflecting the world-leading role that the UK plays in the global creative economy.

"This leadership role for the UK is founded on our deep-rooted talent base, our long tradition of creativity and our business excellence. It is a cornerstone of the UK economy of which we should all be proud."

The government granted planning permission for the multi-million pound film studio following an appeal.

Buckinghamshire Council had previously rejected the project amid concerns about building on protected land.

The project has been backed by Hollywood figures, including Avatar and Titanic director James Cameron, Lord of the Rings actor Andy Serkis and James Bond director Sir Sam Mendes.

The 90-acre development will include 18 sound stages and is expected to create about 2,060 permanent on-site jobs.

Laycock said: "My co-founders and I are delighted to have appointed Sir John and Max and we are looking forward to taking Marlow Studios through its next phase and realising our vision."

articles.title: Who is Katy Marchant? Olympic gold medallist retires at 33 ahead of LA28 Olympics to return to family farm with husband Rob
articles.summary: Katy Marchant has announced her retirement from professional cycling at the age of 33.
articles.body: Katy Marchant has announced her retirement from professional cycling at the age of 33. The Leeds-born track cyclist leaves the sport after a career filled with Olympic, World Championship and European success. Her biggest achievement came at the Paris 2024 Olympics, where she won gold as part of Great Britain’s women’s team sprint squad.Marchant also won an Olympic bronze medal in the individual sprint at Rio 2016. After 13 years at the top level, the mother of two has decided not to continue chasing a place at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. Instead, she will spend more time with her husband Rob and their children on the family farm.Who is Katy Marchant?Katy Marchant was one of Britain’s leading track cyclists for more than a decade. She represented Team GB at three Olympic Games and collected medals across some of the biggest competitions in the sport.Her first Olympic medal came at Rio 2016. Marchant won bronze in the individual sprint and established herself as one of Britain’s leading track sprinters.Eight years later, she reached another major milestone at Paris 2024. Marchant helped Great Britain win gold in the women’s team sprint. The victory completed one of the biggest goals of her career.Her successful 2024 campaign did not end with Olympic gold. Marchant also won gold medals at the World Championships and European Championships.However, her career was also marked by a serious crash in late 2024. She later battled back to professional cycling.Marchant continued competing after becoming a mother of two. She had given birth to her second son a year before this summer’s Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.At the 2026 Commonwealth Games, she won silver in the team sprint. But the event also gave her a feeling that her professional career could be coming to an end.Marchant said, “I’ve done this for 13 years, I am 33, and I have achieved more than I could have dreamt of.”She also explained that retirement had become clear to her, “When I thought about retirement in the past, I said to myself: ‘You’ll know when you know. articles.title: Rumesh Pathirage of Sri Lanka wins javelin at Asian Games. Javelin's a specialty in South Asia
articles.summary: The javelin is often overlooked by casual fans of track and field, but it's a gold-medal specialty in South Asia — specifically for India, Pakistan and now S...
articles.body:
NAGOYA, Japan (AP) — The javelin is often overlooked by casual fans of track and field, but it's a gold-medal specialty in South Asia — specifically for India, Pakistan and now Sri Lanka.

The newest star is Rumesh Pathirage of Sri Lanka, who won the event Monday at the Asian Games under a light drizzle with a throw of 88.33 meters. Yashvir Singh of India took silver (85.14) with bronze for fellow Indian Rohit Yadav (84.35).

Defending Olympic champion Arshad Nadeem of Pakistan was fourth (80.29).

Pathirage is the top thrower this season including a victory in the recent World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, Hungary.

South Asia has seldom delivered gold in the Olympics or other big track meets, but the javelin is different.

Neeraj Chopra of India took gold in the Tokyo Olympics — delayed by the pandemic until 2021. Arshad Nadeem of Pakistan won two years ago in the Paris Olympics. And now it's Pathirage, the No. 1 thrower this season with a personal-best of 92.62.

Despite recent success in the javelin, India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka have been almost invisible at the Olympics.

India has won only 10 gold medals dating from the 1928 Olympics in Amsterdam, eight of them in field hockey. The last Olympic gold was Chopra's in Tokyo. He is out this season with an ankle injury.

Pakistan has only four gold medals in all Olympics, the last was Nadeem's in Paris two years ago.

And Sri Lanka has never won Olympic gold.

That gold-medal scarcity is sure to end when cricket enters the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, and again in 2032 in Brisbane, Australia. It's the only game that really in South Asia.

In addition, India and Qatar are the early favorites to land the 2036 Olympics, which should increase the focus on sports other than cricket.

articles.title: El dominio de la jabalina pasa de Europa a India, Pakistán y Sri Lanka gracias a un deporte muy británico
articles.standfirst: El esrilanqués Rumesh Pathirage completa su gran año con el oro en los Juegos Asiáticos y explica la conexión de su éxito con el críquet
articles.summary: El esrilanqués Rumesh Pathirage completa su gran año con el oro en los Juegos Asiáticos y explica que su éxito se basa en gran medida
articles.body: No hace tanto tiempo, Europa ejercía un dominio casi titánico en el lanzamiento de jabalina. Las escuelas finlandesa y alemana, con sus ramificaciones en los otros países nórdicos y Europa del Este, copaban casi todos los podios olímpicos y mundiales con la excepción de algunos lanzadores británicos o estadounidenses. Este dominio, al menos en categoría masculina, se empezó a resquebrajar con el oro del trinitense Keshorn Walcott en los Juegos de Londres 2012 con apenas 19 años. Walcott lograría un bronce olímpico cuatro años después en Río y el año pasado se proclamó campeón del mundo en Tokio, 13 años después de su histórico triunfo en la capital británica. Ya en los juegos de Tokio 2020, el subcontinente indio lograba su primer gran éxito con el oro del indio Neeraj Chopra, que en París 2024 se debía conformar con la plata a la estela del pakistaní Arshad Nadeem. El granadino Anderson Peters completaba un podio absolutamente impensable hace sólo diez años. En 2026, el protagonismo ha recaído en Rumesh Pathirage, un lanzador de Sri Lanka que ha completado un año prácticamente perfecto con victorias en la final de la Diamond League, el Ultimate Championship de Budapest, los Juegos de la Commonwealth y los Juegos Asiáticos. Precisamente Pathirage hablaba ayer en Nagoya (Japón) tras lograr su victoria en la jabalina de esos Juegos Asiáticos con un mejor lanzamiento de 88,55 metros, por delante de los indios Yashvir Singh (85,14) y Rohit Yadav (84,35). Y lo que dijo no es un secreto para nadie pero ayuda a completar un complejo puzzle que no se entendería sin la impronta del Imperio Británico y su influencia en sus antiguos territorios, más allá del trabajo, claro está, de entrenadores extranjeros como el mítico checo Jan Zelezny -aún plusmarquista mundial-, el ruso Sergey Makarov y el alemán Uwe Hohn, en el caso de Chopra y la creciente escuela india. "El críquet me ha ayudado en mi carrera. Es el mismo movimiento de lanzamiento que en la jabalina, por encima de la cabeza", explicó Pathirage, que al igual que Walcott, Chopra, Nadeem y Peters flirteó con el críquet de joven antes de descubrir su potencial en el atletismo. Pathirage, de momento, se ha situado octavo en la lista de todos los tiempos con un mejor lanzamiento de 92,62 metros pero su gran reto llegará en los Juegos de Los Ángeles 2028, donde intentará lograr el primer oro olímpico de la historia de Sri Lanka. Lo más curioso es que lo hará precisamente en la edición en la que el críquet vuelve a ser olímpico, 128 años después de su primera y única presencia en unos Juegos, los de París 1900. Eso sí, lo hará en su modalidad T20, con partidos más cortos que la modalidad clásica para encajarlos en el apretado calendario olímpico.

articles.title: LA28 Olympic Torch Relay will visit all U.S. states, with symbolic start in Atlanta
articles.summary: Atlanta was the last U.S. city to host the Summer Olympics.
articles.body:
California will take center stage two summers from now when the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles captivates the world's attention. But all 50 states will be represented in the lead-up to those Games.

For the first time , an Olympic Torch Relay will visit every U.S. state, a nationwide journey that will begin in the spring of 2028 and conclude at the Opening Ceremony for LA28.

Fittingly, that expedition will kick off in Atlanta, which hosted the Summer Games in 1996 and is the last U.S. city to do so.

"Every Olympic Games begins with a single flame, and carrying that flame to Los Angeles is an honor and privilege that we'll share with every corner of the country, as Americans in all 50 states carry the flame on its path to our Opening Ceremony," said Casey Wasserman, LA28 chairperson and president, in a Tuesday statement . "Starting this journey in Atlanta is a tribute to a city with deep Olympic roots and to partners like Coca-Cola, whose support has helped carry this Movement for a century. Coca-Cola, JPMorganChase, Allstate and Xfinity, along with participating cities, are making these Relays possible, and in the months ahead, we look forward to welcoming even more cities and partners to this historic moment for our country."

"Starting this journey in Atlanta is a tribute to a city with deep Olympic roots and to partners like Coca-Cola, whose support has helped carry this Movement for a century. Coca-Cola, JPMorganChase, Allstate and Xfinity, along with participating cities, are making these Relays possible, and in the months ahead, we look forward to welcoming even more cities and partners to this historic moment for our country."

Coca-Cola's partnership with the Olympics started in 1928 . Famously, the World of Coca-Cola museum neighbors Atlanta's Centennial Olympic Park, which was constructed ahead of the 1996 Olympics.

Before the Olympic flame is stateside, it will be lit in Olympia, Greece. The complete route for the LA28 Olympic Torch Relay will be announced in 2027.

The 2028 Olympics will run from July 14-30. Then the Paralympic Games will take place from Aug. 15-27.

Atlanta mayor Andre Dickens said in a statement Tuesday that the city "will be ready" for the flame to return.

"Thirty years ago, Atlanta welcomed the world," Dickens said. "The 1996 Centennial Olympic Games changed this city. They introduced a modern Atlanta to billions of people across the globe and proved we could compete on the biggest international stage.

"Thirty years later, Atlanta looks a little different. We are bigger. We are more connected to the world. So, when the flame returns to the U.S., Atlanta will be ready. Ready to welcome it from Greece. Ready to celebrate the spirit of the Games together as a community. And ready to send it forward toward Los Angeles and the next chapter of America's Olympic story."

Dickens added in that statement: "Atlanta was proud to carry that flame in 1996. We will be proud to welcome it back."

articles.title: Simone Biles Talks Possibility of Competing in 2028 LA Olympics, Explains Factors for Decision
articles.summary: Simone Biles still isn't closing the door on competing in the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles.
articles.body:
Simone Biles still isn't closing the door on competing in the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles.

"I'm like 'Oh my gosh, I don't know what the decision (is) I should make,' but I don't necessarily have to make it just yet," she told the Associated Press' Will Graves . "But I feel like it's kind of in the works which way I'm leaning towards."

Biles explained how her considerations now are far different than they were in previous Olympic cycles.

Broncos OL Drug Tested After Viral Clip 🎥

"I am getting to the age of 30 where we start to talk about, 'What does your reproduction cycle ... what's going on in there? What does that look like? How healthy is it?'" she said. "And so I think these are major things that are on the table at my age that I have to take in consideration and weigh those options and what that looks like and when we want to start a family."

Biles already defied the odds by winning three gold medals and one silver in the 2024 Summer Olympics in Paris. She was the oldest female gymnast (27) to be the all-around champion since Maria Gorokhovskaya in 1952.

A gymnast competing in four Olympics isn't unprecedented but certainly uncommon.

Beyond padding her already substantial legacy, the 2028 Summer Olympics would present Biles with the chance to win gold on home soil. The United States hasn't hosted the Summer Games since 1996.

"Like a home Olympic Games, like, how could you not?" she said to Graves. "It's absolutely incredible."

Biles got fans excited last month when she posted photos from her regular training gym, World Champions Centre in Texas.

While she was far from definitive in her interview with Graves, the fact she's still considering 2028 leads you to believe the 11-time Olympic medalist is leaning toward a return.

articles.title: Parents of Arizona State Hockey Player Who Collapses Call for Coaches to Be Placed on Leave
articles.summary: TEMPE, Ariz. (AP) — The parents of an Arizona State hockey player who collapsed during an outdoor workout are calling for the coaches involved to be removed until an independent investigation is completed.
articles.body:
TEMPE, Ariz. (AP) — The parents of an Arizona State hockey player who collapsed during an outdoor workout are calling for the coaches involved to be removed until an independent investigation is completed.

John and Christina Mayich, parents of 21-year-old Matthew Mayich, released a statement through the family attorney on Tuesday, concurring with a letter sent by seven Arizona State hockey players to university president Michael Crow on Monday. The players asked the university to place the coaches involved in the Aug. 20 workout to be placed on administrative leave until an investigation by an outside agency is completed.

The letter was sent anonymously through an attorney because the players feared retribution from the coaching staff.

"We've heard some things about what our family wants that aren't right, so we want to be clear: we want this team to have a great season and we'll be cheering for you," the Mayichs said through attorney Rob Carey. "But the coaches who ran that workout on August 20 need to be removed while an independent investigation gets to the truth. The players shouldn't have to worry about retaliation from the people they report to every day."

Mayich, a 21-year-old defenseman who was drafted by the St. Louis Blues, collapsed during an outdoor workout on the first day the NCAA allows official activities. He suffered from external heat stroke that reduced flow of oxygen to his brain and is unlikely to recover, Carey said.

The letter sent by the players called out discrepancies from an initial probe by Arizona State and asked for an interim coaching staff be put in place if the coaches involved are placed on leave.

"Nobody should keep quiet about what they think should happen because they believe that's what we want. It isn't," the Mayichs said. "If anyone wants to know what we want, ask us. We want the truth, and we want it done in a way that lets the boys focus on hockey instead of wondering whether their coaches think they talked. Mostly, we want accountability for what happened to our son, and we want his teammates to be safe."

The Arizona State police department is investigating the incident and a report will be sent to the Maricopa County Attorney's Office for independent review when completed.

Arizona's House and Senate education committee chairs called for an independent investigation of Arizona State's hockey workout after reading the letter from the players.

articles.body:
The torch relay ahead of the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028 will pass through all 50 US states for the first time, starting with Georgia, organizers said Tuesday.

The route will begin in Atlanta -- the most recent US city to host a Summer Olympics, back in 1996 -- before finishing in California.

"Every Olympic Games begins with a single flame, and carrying that flame to Los Angeles is an honor and privilege that we'll share with every corner of the country, as Americans in all 50 states carry the flame on its path to our Opening Ceremony," said LA28 president Casey Wasserman.

Full details of the route, which will begin in spring of 2028, are still being planned and will be unveiled next year.

As is tradition, the Olympic flame will first be lit in Olympia, Greece --- the birthplace of the ancient Olympic Games.

It will then be flown to Atlanta, before beginning its epic American road trip. The LA28 Olympic Games will run from July 14-30.

In 1996, the torch visited 42 states, and memorably went to space aboard the Space Shuttle Columbia. For the 1984 Los Angeles Games, the relay toured 33 states.
